name: Piroctone olamine

lead: Piroctone olamine is an antifungal ingredient in many anti-dandruff shampoos. It targets the Malassezia yeasts linked to flaking and itch.
Studies have compared it with zinc pyrithione and ketoconazole shampoos for dandruff and shedding; it is a scalp-condition ingredient rather than a hair-growth treatment.

paras: It is thought to enter fungal cells and bind iron, disrupting energy production; the exact mechanism is not fully established.
EU rules cap it at 1.0% in rinse-off and 0.5% in other cosmetics. Labels advise avoiding eyes and stopping use if irritation or allergy occurs.

lead: Piroctone olamine is the ethanolamine salt of piroctone, a hydroxypyridone-type antifungal used mainly in anti-dandruff shampoos and scalp-care products. It is sold by Clariant as Octopirox.[1][2]

It is aimed at Malassezia yeasts associated with dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis.[3] Several comparative trials have tested piroctone olamine shampoos against zinc pyrithione shampoos.[4][5] In the EU it is permitted as a cosmetic ingredient up to 1.0% in rinse-off and 0.5% in other products.[2]
infobox: Cosmetic ingredient in the EU; OTC dandruff active in some US products[6]

paras: The main use is dandruff and mild seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, in shampoos and conditioners.[1][2] A US-listed over-the-counter product combines piroctone olamine with salicylic acid for dandruff; its label says it helps prevent recurrence of flaking and itching and advises against use on broken or inflamed scalp or in children under 12.[6]

It is generally described as an antifungal acting against Malassezia. Proposed mechanisms include penetrating the fungal membrane and chelating iron, which interferes with mitochondrial energy metabolism, or inhibiting ergosterol synthesis; the exact mechanism is not fully established.[1][2]

Regulators in the EU list it in Annex V of the Cosmetics Regulation with the maximum concentrations above.[2] The product label cited above warns of external use only, avoiding eyes, and stopping use if an allergic reaction or irritation persists.[6]

A 2011 randomised comparison tested a shampoo with 0.5% piroctone olamine and 0.45% climbazole against a 1% zinc pyrithione shampoo in people with moderate to severe dandruff.[4] A 2000 study compared a piroctone olamine and salicylic acid shampoo with a zinc pyrithione shampoo.[5] A 2002 study compared 1% ketoconazole, 1% piroctone olamine and 1% zinc pyrithione shampoos for effects on hair shedding.[7] A 2017 randomised comparative trial examined Malassezia populations on seborrheic dermatitis scalps.[8] A 2022 review of seborrheic dermatitis management covers antifungal shampoos generally.[3]
Registered studies include a 2025 trial of a 0.75% piroctone olamine shampoo on scalp microbiota in women with seborrheic dermatitis (NCT07802808).[9]

timeline.event: First synthesised by Schwarzkopf-Henkel, according to later published sources.[2]
